newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Wealthy "new Romanians" divided in election race.
newsitem.headline: Wealthy "new Romanians" divided in election race.

text.p: Wealthy "new Romanians" who have made quick fortunes in seven years of embryonic capitalism face a dilemma in this weekend's general election.
Should they back President Ion Iliescu and his Party for Social Democracy (PDSR), former Communists uncommitted to rapid reform but who still provided business opportunities?
Or the liberal opposition which promises to change laws and foster free enterprise?
"These people will not only vote for the PDSR, they will be donating millions to the party's campaign," said Dorel Sandor, head of the independent Institute for Political Studies.
"A change in regime would not only mean losing privileges but also running the risk of being brought to justice."
Some leading businessmen disagree.

"My company would have progressed much more had legislation allowed it," Viorel Catarama, president and main shareholder of furniture maker Elvila International, said at the firm's $20 million glass and marble headquarters.
"The laws here are against the private sector. The government constantly discrimates against private companies."

Iliescu, who says moderate reforms have minimised social costs, leads opinion polls ahead of Sunday's election but is likely to be forced to a run-off later this month. His party trails the opposition in polls for elections to parliament.

As in all post-Communist societies, the number of New Romanians is tiny -- sociologists say no more than 10,000 -- while statistics show some 4.5 million people have been hurled into poverty by the transition to the market.
Ordinary Romanians bitterly resent their very visible lifestyle -- luxurious cars and foreign-designed wardrobes, mobile telephones always ready to hand.
Some build vast three-storey houses on the outskirts of Bucharest. Others bankroll soccer teams, luring top quality players with promises of houses or fat bonuses.
Iliescu has taken great care during the campaign to distance himself and his party from newly-acquired wealth.

"Within the Party of Social Democracy leadership, there is not a single one of the famous 'nouveau riche' who have appeared after the revolution," he told a television interviewer. "The opposition parties have lots of them."
But many people have concluded that wealth has settled alongside political power.

"The middle class or big industry, trade and banking tycoons could not have acquired their fortunes without the help of people in power," analyst and former senior Communist Silviu Brucan wrote in his recent book "The Pillars of the New Power".
Voters of the opposition Democratic Convention raised some of their loudest jeers in a Bucharest march when they passed the Lido hotel, one of several owned by tycoon George Paunescu.
Paunescu had a top job in the trade ministry during the tenure of executed dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

Newspapers allege he retains links with the government. Paunescu denies it, saying he got his small trading business off the ground in 1990 by making use of old contacts and borrowing 100,000 lei, enough to buy a two-room flat at the time.
"I was in an unique position to take advantage of opportunities created by an incompetent government," Paunescu told the magazine Central European Business last year.
A few wealthy businessmen have clearly aligned themselves with the opposition, like Dinu Patriciu, leader of the Liberal Party '93, who is running for a seat in parliament on Sunday.
"It's those businessmen who have had to fight against state bureaucracy and privilege who will vote for the opposition," Sandor said.
